findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:89 (`v.prefix = cls.PREFIX` in LeverSet.__init_subclass__)
findings.problem: `__init_subclass__` MUTATES the shared `Lever` object rather than recording the prefix per owning class. Two verified consequences, both of which pass all seven O-checks. (a) SHARED INSTANCE: a module-level `POOL = Lever(4096, ...)` used as a field in two LeverSets ends up with ONE env name — whichever class was defined last. Measured: `ALevers.env_names()` and `BLevers.env_names()` both return `{'BBB_POOL'}`; setting `BBB_POOL=7` moves BOTH packages; `AAA_POOL` is dead forever and `registry.unread_env({'AAA_POOL':'7'})` returns `[]` because the registry still holds the stale `AAA_POOL -> AAA` row written before the mutation. affects('BBB_POOL')={'BBB'} (understates), affects('AAA_POOL')={'AAA'} (a lever whose measured reach is empty, so L3's subset test passes it). A cross-package coupling with no wire, no `d_` field, no ledger edge, no budget line, and no static or behavioural detection. (b) SUBCLASS: `class Shadow(FabricLevers): PREFIX='SHD'` rewrites the PARENT's env names — measured `FabricLevers.env_names()` goes from `{FAB_SLOTS,FAB_PRESSURE,FAB_MANAGE_EVERY}` to `{SHD_*}` the moment the child module is imported. `FAB_SLOTS` silently stops working; `SHD_SLOTS=22` now drives the fabric. O3 catches the naive spelling only because the child names two LeverSets; with `from fabric.levers import FabricLevers as _Base` all seven checks PASS (verified). This is not only an attack — it is a live bug that breaks an innocent intermediate base class, which `_leversets()`'s own fixed-point loop says it expects to see.
findings.fix: Never write to the Lever. Bind the prefix per (class, field): keep `cls._levers = {name: (lever, cls.PREFIX)}`, or copy the Lever in `__init_subclass__`, and make `env_name(prefix)` take the prefix as an argument instead of reading `self.prefix`. Then add two refusals in `__init_subclass__`: reject a Lever object already bound to a different owner (LeverError naming both classes and both env names), and reject a subclass whose PREFIX differs from a base that already declared levers unless every inherited lever is re-declared. Add an O-check that no `Lever(...)` is assigned at module level outside a class body.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:148 (`Config.__getattr__`) and :132 (`Config._wire`)
findings.problem: A LEVER whose field name starts with `d_` silently SHADOWS the wire of the same name. `__getattr__` resolves `self._vals` before `self._wired`, and `_wire` checks only the frozen flag and the `d_` prefix — never whether the name is already a declared lever. Verified end to end: `MemoryLevers` declaring `d_capacity = Lever(200000, ...)` gives env name `MEM_D_CAPACITY`; `assemble.build()` computes the coupling's value (8192) and stores it; the package reads `cfg.d_capacity` and gets 200000. `cfg.wired()` and therefore `render()` / docs/03_WIRING.md print 8192 — the printed coupling graph and the running system describe different systems, which is what `Wires.add`'s duplicate-destination guard and `_check_table` exist to prevent, reached from the one direction neither of them watches. All seven checks PASS; the only trace is `keys()` returning a list with `d_capacity` twice, and nothing reads it. It reproduces exactly the memory.py:36 defect that this coupling's own `why` describes: a declared capacity silently overriding a derived one.
findings.fix: Refuse the collision at both ends. In `Lever.__set_name__` (or `__init_subclass__`), raise LeverError on any field name starting `d_`: the `d_` namespace belongs to the wire. In `Config._wire`, raise if `name in self._vals`. Assert `len(keys()) == len(set(keys()))` in `_freeze()` so the invariant is checked once per run rather than trusted.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:140-142 (`Config._freeze`), :122 (`__slots__`)
findings.problem: Frozen is a flag, not a state. `_freeze()` sets `_frozen=True`, which only `_wire` consults; `_vals` and `_wired` remain ordinary dicts on public slots that normal attribute lookup reaches (they never hit `__getattr__`, so its leading-underscore guard is irrelevant). Verified on a frozen Config: `c.slots = 8` raises LeverError as designed, but `c._vals['slots'] = 8` succeeds and `c.slots` then returns 8, and `c._wired['d_anything'] = 1` injects a wired field with no ledger row, no budget line, and no coupling. Nothing static sees it: not a `d_` attribute write (O4 looks for `x.d_foo` in Store context), not a module-level mutable global (O5), not an environment read (O1). This defeats the guarantee the spine is sold on — 'there is no re-read, so the report reads the same object the run used' (lever.py:23-24) — with a one-line spelling that reads as ordinary Python.
findings.fix: Make the freeze real: at `_freeze()`, replace `_vals` and `_wired` with `types.MappingProxyType` over copies (cheap, and `__getattr__`'s `.get()` still works), or rebuild them as tuples of pairs. Independently add an O-check that `._vals`, `._wired` and `._frozen` are named nowhere outside `src/spine/lever.py` and `src/spine/assemble.py` — a two-line AST rule that closes the plain spelling even if the proxy is later removed.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:165 (`Config.lever`) and :35-51 (`Lever` has no `__setattr__` guard)
findings.problem: `Config.lever(k)` hands out the live declaration object. `Lever` has `__slots__` but nothing frozen about it, so `cfg.lever('n').default = 99` rewrites the single declared default for every subsequent `from_env()` in the process. Verified: after mutating through a Config, `T.from_env({}).n` returns 99. L1 says 'one literal default, no second default anywhere' and O2 enforces it at author time; at run time the one default is a writable attribute reachable from any package's own Config. Combined with the O3 alias hole below (one foreign LeverSet import is legal), a package can rewrite another package's defaults.
findings.fix: Freeze the Lever once `__set_name__` has run — a `__setattr__` that raises LeverError after `name` is set — or have `Config.lever()` return a read-only namedtuple view (default, help, unit, choices, env_name) rather than the declaration itself. Nothing outside `lever.py` needs the mutable object.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py docstring lines 12-14 and src/spine/assemble.py:3-6 (the claim), enforced nowhere
findings.problem: The load-bearing structural claim is false. Both docstrings state that a package receives only its own record so 'reading a foreign lever is a NameError at author time, not a policy'. `build()` returns `{PREFIX: Config}` and a Config carries no owner check at the point of use, so passing `configs['FAB']` into a memory function as an ordinary parameter gives full read access to every FAB lever. Verified: `def evict(cfg, peer): return peer.slots // cfg.owners, peer.pressure` in `src/memory/use.py` reads FAB_SLOTS=999 and FAB_PRESSURE=0.9 with no import, no alias, no `d_` field — all seven checks PASS and `affects('FAB_PRESSURE')` stays `{'FAB'}`. O3's and O4's CANNOT-CATCH notes each concede half of this, but the docstrings still assert the guarantee as a structural fact rather than as something only L3 can see — and L3 sees it only when the foreign value moves an integer fingerprint, so a foreign lever consumed on a report or instrument path is invisible to every check in the tree.
findings.fix: First, stop asserting it as structural in the docstrings — that sentence is the reason a reviewer will not look. Then make it enforceable: give each package an entry accessor that asserts `cfg.prefix == MY_PREFIX`, or hand packages a `_Fields`-style restricted view (assemble.py already builds exactly this machinery for `compute`). At minimum, add an O-check that no function outside the wiring file takes two parameters both annotated as Configs, and that `build()`'s return value is not subscripted outside `bin/`.

findings.where: tests/test_ownership.py:341 (`_leversets` keys on the class name) and :388 (`check_o3` matches `ast.Name.id` against those names)
findings.problem: O3 is defeated by a local alias, and one foreign lever set is legal anyway, so the two combine into a complete bypass. Verified: `src/memory/policy.py` containing `from fabric.levers import FabricLevers as _F` and `_F.from_env().slots` passes all seven checks and reads FAB_SLOTS=999 at will. Two distinct defects. (a) The alias: `_leversets()` is keyed by CLASS name and `check_o3` looks for that name in scope, so any `as` rename is invisible — measured directly, the aliased-subclass case that FAILS O3 unaliased PASSES aliased. `_imports()` already computes the local-name -> (module, original) map that would fix this, and O3 does not use it. (b) `from_env()` is a public classmethod on every LeverSet, callable from anywhere, and it re-reads `os.environ` mid-run — so the foreign read also defeats 'resolved once, frozen', is invisible to `build()`'s typo net and to the read audit, and can return a value differing from the one the report prints if the harness mutates the environment between arms.
findings.fix: Resolve aliases: in `check_o3`, count lever sets by RESOLVED origin using `_imports()`'s `names` map, not by the local spelling, and do the same on the `ast.Attribute` path. Add an eighth check: `LeverSet.from_env` may be called only from `src/spine/assemble.py` — the same one-file rule O1 applies to `os.environ`, and the rule that actually makes 'resolved once' true.

findings.where: src/spine/assemble.py:165-215 (`_Fields` / `_Reads`), used at :548 (`value = c.compute(_view(c, configs))`)
findings.problem: Mechanism 2 restricts only the `r` argument, not the closure. Any helper called from inside `compute` reads whatever it likes. Verified: changing one row to `compute=lambda r: max(64, 2*int(r['FAB'].slots)) + _peek()`, where `_peek()` does `from fabric.levers import FabricLevers; return int(FabricLevers.from_env().manage_every)`, leaves all seven checks PASSING, makes `MEM.d_source_slots` move with `FAB_MANAGE_EVERY`, and leaves `affects('FAB_MANAGE_EVERY') = {'FAB'}`. The module docstring claims 'the declared `reads` set is therefore enforced rather than advisory' — it is advisory for anything not arriving through `r`. L3 catches the fingerprint-visible half but reports it as MEM leaking rather than as assemble under-declaring, sending the investigation to the wrong package.
findings.fix: Check `compute`'s free names at Coupling construction: `compute.__code__.co_names` and `co_freevars` must be empty except for a small allowlist of pure helpers declared in one place (today `_owner_blocks` and `derive.*`). Five lines, runs at import on a machine with no environment set, and it makes the declared `reads` set genuinely enforced. Pair with an O-check that `from_env` is not named inside `assemble.py` outside `build()`.

findings.where: tests/test_ownership.py:288 (`_calls_named` matches the literal name `Coupling`), :483 (`_d_field_uses` matches only `ast.Attribute`/literal `getattr`), and the live-vs-AST cross-check inside `check_o4_wires_match_reads`
findings.problem: O4 has two independent plain-Python evasions that combine into a second coupling table nobody sees. (a) `_C = assemble.Coupling` then `_T.append(_C(...))` is not a `Coupling(` call to the AST, so the 'Coupling declared outside the wiring file' finding, the O6 reason check, and the AST-vs-live ledger cross-check all go quiet — and `_T = assemble.COUPLINGS` is the alias launder O5's own CANNOT-CATCH note admits it cannot follow. (b) `cfg.wired()['d_pressure_bias']` reads a wired field through a Subscript, which `_d_field_uses` does not look at; `cfg.keys()` and `cfg.given()` are the same hole. Verified together: `src/memory/extra.py` appending a full FAB.pressure -> MEM.d_pressure_bias coupling at import, read through `wired()` in `src/memory/use.py`, gives 7 checks / 0 failing while the coupling is live at runtime. Separately, the cross-check meant to guarantee 'the ledger this test reads is the one the run uses' imports only `spine.assemble` and never the packages, so a coupling appended from a package module cannot be seen by it even in principle.
findings.fix: Resolve `Coupling` and `COUPLINGS` by import origin (same `_imports()` fix as O3), and flag ANY reference to either name outside the wiring file rather than only call sites. Treat `.wired()`, `.keys()` and `.given()` subscripted by a `d_` string literal as a d_ read. For the cross-check, walk `src/*/` and import every package before comparing tables — otherwise its population is whatever `spine.assemble` happens to pull in.

findings.where: tests/test_ownership.py:58 (`SRC = os.path.join(ROOT, 'src')`) and the O1 hit set in `check_o1_one_env_reader`
findings.problem: O1 only scans `src/`. PLAN P7 delivers `bin/` and P2/G10 deliver `tools/`, and neither is walked — so the harness, which is exactly where the arm table lives and therefore the most natural place to launder a lever, may name any environment variable and hand the value to any package. Verified: `bin/train.py` with `nmax = int(os.environ.get('FAB_SLOTS','4096'))` leaves O1 green at '1 environment reference(s) in 1 file(s)'. Second hole in the same check: `vars(os)['environ']` is not caught even with a plain string literal — the CANNOT-CATCH note concedes only a COMPUTED `getattr`, and `vars(os)[...]` / `os.__dict__[...]` is neither exotic nor computed. Verified: `_E = vars(os)['envi' 'ron']` in a package module passes O1.
findings.fix: Walk `bin/`, `tools/` and `tests/` as well as `src/`, keeping `src/spine/lever.py` as the sole permitted reader, and add `vars(...)` / `.__dict__` subscripted by an ENV_NAMES literal to the hit set. If `bin/` genuinely needs the mapping to pass into `build(environ=...)`, name that one file as a second permitted reader explicitly — an exception with a name is reviewable; an unscanned directory is not.

findings.where: src/spine/units.py:69 (`Clock.__eq__`) and `check_o7_no_clock_vs_int` in tests/test_ownership.py
findings.problem: Every ordering operator on a Clock raises UnitError; equality silently answers. Verified: `Steps(4000) == 250` is False, `Steps(0) == 0` is False, `Steps(4000) == Flushes(4000)` is False, and `!=` is True in all three. Given this project's history — SIG_WIN's 0 sentinel resolving to 614 bytes in one path and 1 byte in another — `if period == 0: period = derived` is the idiom this codebase actually writes, and against a Clock it now takes the wrong branch on every step forever: the untrippable-guard shape (60 of 475 records) reintroduced by the module written to kill it. O7 does not cover it either — it only flags a Compare where one operand is a literal AND another is a Clock CONSTRUCTION CALL, so `cfg.d_manage_period == 0` is invisible statically as well. Related and lower: `__index__` lets `list[Flushes(2):Steps(5)]` slice silently across kinds.
findings.fix: Make `__eq__` raise UnitError against a bare int/float (the case with measured history), returning False only for a different Clock kind if total equality is needed for dict/set use; define `__ne__` to match. Extend O7 to flag `== 0` / `!= 0` and `== <literal>` on any name matching `*_period` / `*_every` / `d_*_period` — cheap, and it catches the named-threshold form the check currently concedes it cannot see.

findings.where: src/spine/assemble.py:498 (`build(..., budget=None)`) and src/spine/wire.py:54 (WIRE_BUDGET)
findings.problem: WIRE_BUDGET's stated job is that 'somebody has to change this number in a commit, and that shows up in review'. `budget` is a public parameter of `build()`, and no check scans `bin/`, so `assemble.build(os.environ, budget=999)` in the harness raises the budget with nothing in the diff touching wire.py and nothing in the ownership pass looking. The docstring's 'it is a parameter only so a test can prove the budget bites' is true of the intent and not of the surface.
findings.fix: Make `budget` keyword-only and refuse any value above `wire.WIRE_BUDGET` unless an explicit `over_budget_reason` string is also passed and printed by `render()`; or drop the parameter entirely and let tests construct `Wires(budget=n)` directly — they already have that path.

findings.where: src/spine/registry.py:49 (`fams = tuple(families or sorted({p + '_' for p in _SETS}))`)
findings.problem: The typo net (G9) is blind to the most common typo. `unread_env` skips any name that does not already start with a declared `PREFIX_`, so a misspelling in the PREFIX half — the half that carries ownership — is reported as nothing at all. Verified against a registered PREFIX 'ZZ': `unread_env({'ZZZ_N':'9'})` returns `[]` and `unread_env({'ZZN':'9'})` returns `[]`, while `ZZ_NN` is correctly reported. The docstring says its job is that 'a mis-typed knob is silently the default, and this project has lost runs to exactly that'; `FBA_SLOTS`, `FABSLOTS` and `FAB2_SLOTS` are all silently the default and all invisible.
findings.fix: Add a second pass over every UPPERCASE environment name not in the known set: report any whose edit distance to a declared lever name is <= 2 (the `_dist` helper already exists), scored against the full name rather than filtered by family first. Keep the family filter only as the ordering hint it is good at.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:65 (`Lever.coerce`, the bool branch)
findings.problem: A flag is True unless the raw string is exactly one of ('0','','off','no','none','false'). Verified: `ZZ_FLAG=0.0` resolves to True. So do `disabled`, `f`, and any numeric-zero spelling an arm table or shell template produces. Every other coercion failure in this class is fatal at startup by name; this is the single case that silently resolves to the opposite of what was written, and a switch reading ON when the operator wrote 0.0 is the armed-but-inert class (57 of 475 records) arriving from the configuration side.
findings.fix: Declare the truthy set as well ('1','on','yes','true') and raise LeverError naming the lever and the raw value for anything in neither — the same failure shape `int(float(raw))` already gives. A flag with an unrecognised value is a declaration fault, not a default.

findings.where: tests/_noise_floor.json (`floor.abs`, `floor.rel`), read by `load_floor` in tests/test_determinism.py:818
findings.problem: L3's verdict is stated against a checked-in JSON file whose float floor can be hand-raised to any value. The machine-identity key covers the MACHINE fields, not the floor block, so an edited floor still loads cleanly on the machine that wrote it. Measured floor today is abs 0.0 / rel 0.0, so any nonzero edit is pure slack. Mitigating and worth stating in the report: the integer half is protected — the floor is REFUSED outright if integer fingerprints were unstable — and L3's headline comparison is on integer fingerprints, so this weakens only the float half.
findings.fix: Fold a digest of the raw per-pair measurements into the record and have `load_floor` recompute it, refusing a floor whose stated value does not follow from the measurements beside it. Cheaper interim: have `load_floor(require_usable=True)` refuse a floor above a declared sanity bound and print the refusal, so a raised floor is a loud failure rather than quiet slack.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:54 (`Lever.__set_name__`)
findings.problem: `x = y = Lever(2048, ...)` inside one LeverSet calls `__set_name__` twice on one object; the last name wins, so `_levers` holds two keys pointing at one Lever with one env name. Both `cfg.x` and `cfg.y` then resolve from a single environment variable and one of the two declared knob names is dead — the same root cause as the critical finding above: the Lever carries identity that belongs to the (class, field) pair.
findings.fix: Covered by the critical finding's fix if identity moves off the Lever; otherwise raise in `__set_name__` when `self.name` is already set to a different name.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:86-91 (LeverSet.__init_subclass__, `v.prefix = cls.PREFIX`)
findings.fix: Stop mutating the Lever. Store the binding on the owner, not on the shared object: build `cls._levers = {k: (v, cls.PREFIX)}`, or copy the Lever in __init_subclass__ before setting .prefix, and make env_name take the owning prefix as an argument (`lv.env_name_for(cls.PREFIX)`) so one Lever instance can legally serve two owners. Add a test that declares a base with a lever plus a subclass with a different PREFIX and asserts both env_names() sets are still correct after the second class is defined.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:148 (Config.__getattr__) with src/spine/lever.py:35-59 (Lever) -- nothing refuses a d_-prefixed lever NAME
findings.problem:
__getattr__ resolves `self._vals` BEFORE `self._wired`, and no code anywhere refuses a Lever whose field name starts with d_. So a receiving package can declare `d_capacity = Lever(999, ...)` and silently shadow the wire that writes that exact field. Reproduced end to end through assemble.build():

  wire recorded value  : 1000
  cfg.wired()          : {'d_capacity': 1000}
  cfg.d_capacity       : 999          <-- every consumer reads the local default
  cfg.keys()           : ['d_capacity', 'd_capacity']
  assemble.render()    : prints the row as RESOLVED = 1000

This is exactly the laundering finding G5 exists to answer, arrived at from the receiver's side: the wire names the field, but the receiver can pre-empt the name. The ledger, render(), affects() and the O4 static audit all agree the coupling landed; the running system uses a different number. Silent-overwrite is the class the project counts 29 records of, and this instance leaves a ledger that positively asserts the wrong thing.
findings.fix: Refuse the name at declaration: in Lever.__set_name__ (or LeverSet.__init_subclass__) raise LeverError if the field starts with 'd_' -- a d_ name means 'arrived by wire' and a lever can never be one. Belt and braces: make Config._wire raise if `name in self._vals`, and have Config.keys() assert its two sources are disjoint.

findings.where: src/spine/derive.py:265-285 (pin_tick) and .rework/oracle/pin_tick.json / tests/test_derive.py:166
findings.problem:
pin_tick is the function reproducing the project's flagship unit defect, and it is the one function in derive.py with no unit typing at all. flush_period and accum_due reject foreign clocks; pin_tick accepts anything: `pin_tick(Flushes(2650), True, Flushes(16))` -> 2666 (a bare int labelled 'steps'), `pin_tick(True, 400, 16)` -> 17.

Worse, its oracle cannot see the defect either. The capture grid is `[(h,p,d) for h in (True, False) ...]` -- held is a BOOLEAN in all 32 cases. I wrote the exact defect the docstring names ('IT MUST BE A STEP DELTA AND IT WAS A BARE +1/-1') as `h = 1 if held else 0` and it passes 32 of 32 oracle cases. Only one hand-written smoke line, `pin_tick(2650, True, 16) == 2666`, catches it. And nothing anywhere -- table or smoke -- exercises the decrement branch with held > 1, so the documented 'clamped at zero on the way down' behaviour is asserted by no test: an impostor returning `0` for the whole unpinned branch fails only 1 of 32 cases and passes smoke.
findings.fix: Type the arguments: accept `held` and `dstep` as Steps and return Steps (keep positional order for the oracle, and coerce ints at the boundary so the 32 captured cases still replay). Add smoke assertions for the decrement path with a real accumulated clock -- pin_tick(2650, False, 16) == 2634 and pin_tick(10, False, 100) == 0 -- and assert that a Flushes in the held slot raises.

findings.where: src/spine/units.py:69-71 (Clock.__eq__)
findings.problem:
__eq__ returns NotImplemented for non-Clock and plain False for a different Clock kind, while <, <=, >, >= all raise UnitError. Measured:

  Flushes(10) == Steps(10)  -> False   (no raise)
  Steps(4000) == 4000       -> False
  Steps(0)    == 0          -> False
  Flushes(10) != Steps(10)  -> True

The module docstring says the whole mechanism is that a cross-kind comparison raises. Equality is a cadence idiom this codebase actually uses (`if held == period`, `if n == 0`), and in that form a mismatched clock produces a guard whose condition can never be satisfied -- silently, forever. That is the untrippable-guard class the file was written to remove, reintroduced through the one operator that was exempted.
findings.fix: Route __eq__ through _same for the Clock-vs-Clock case (raise on a kind mismatch) and for numeric operands (int/float/bool), keeping NotImplemented only for genuinely unrelated types so `clock in some_list` still behaves. tests/test_derive.py:142 relies on `Flushes(1250) == Flushes(1250)`, which stays legal. Add the negative cases to the smoke block alongside the existing UnitError checks.

findings.where: src/spine/assemble.py:498 (build), 586 (render); src/spine/wire.py:323 (affects), 370 (render); src/spine/registry.py:216 (unread_env); src/spine/rng.py:326 (issued)
findings.problem: The entire runtime spine is armed and unreached by the test suite. grep over tests/ shows no call to assemble.build(), assemble.render(), Wires.affects(), Wires.render(), registry.unread_env() or rng.issued(). tests/test_ownership.py touches assemble only to read `assemble.COUPLINGS` for the AST cross-check; tests/test_determinism.py mentions build() only inside a comment marking the P3 plug point. wire.py:270-276 cites 'the smoke exercise, which counted five wires after four successful add() calls' as the thing that found an ordering bug -- that exercise is not in the tree. I exercised build() by hand with six stand-in LeverSets and it works correctly (8 wires, correct affects() sets, correct typo warning), but nothing in the repo would notice if it stopped: G1's oracle, G5's assignment path and G9's typo net are all currently proven only by reading.
findings.fix: Add tests/test_assemble.py: declare stand-in LeverSets for the six prefixes the table names, call build(environ={...}) with one correct knob, one misspelled knob and one foreign name, and assert the wired values, the DEFERRED warnings, the UNREAD warning, the affects() set for one lever of each package, that render() is non-empty, and that the budget and the frozen-Config refusals trip. It is roughly 60 lines and it converts every claim above from prose to a check.

findings.where: src/spine/wire.py:131-137 and :202 (_check_unit / Wire.__init__); src/spine/assemble.py:133 (Coupling.__init__)
findings.problem: A wire records a unit and never compares it to the value it carries. Reproduced: `wires.add('TRAIN.batch_w', 'FAB.d_period', Steps(1250), '<reason>', U.Flushes)` is accepted and the ledger, render() and docs/03_WIRING.md all say 'flushes' over a Steps value. wire.py's own comment at :120-124 says a wire 'is precisely where a unit mismatch is invisible: the value arrives already computed, under a name the receiver did not choose, and the receiver has no declaration to compare it against.' Clock kinds are runtime types specifically so this case is checkable, and it is the only place in the spine where a declared unit is decorative rather than enforced. Today all four Flushes wires happen to be correct; nothing keeps them so.
findings.fix: In _check_unit, keep returning the KIND string but also return the class, and in Wire.__init__ / Coupling resolution raise WireError when `unit` is a Clock subclass and `type(value) is not unit`. Non-clock units stay metadata as designed.

findings.where: src/spine/derive.py:109 (`return min(n_slots, n) if n_slots >= 3 else n_slots`)
findings.problem: operating_population's `n = max(3, n)` floor is thrown away for slots < 3, and the raw input is returned instead. Measured: operating_population(0.5, 0) -> 0, (0.5, 2) -> 2, (0.5, -5) -> -5. Every one of those is a 'setpoint' at which cull_gate_open can never open (n_live <= 2 shuts it), so the docstring's stated property -- 'cull_gate_open(operating_population(p,s), s, p) is True' -- is false there. tests/test_derive.py:113 only sweeps slots in (4,100,1024,4096,8192) and asserts `3 <= n <= slots`, which would fail immediately if slots<3 were in the grid. I brute-forced slots 0..40 plus the large values: for slots >= 3 the consistency claim holds with zero violations, so the defect is confined to the degenerate tail that the test deliberately avoids.
findings.fix: Decide and state which it is. Either raise on slots < 3 ('a fabric with fewer than three slots has no equilibrium population'), or return max(3, ...) unconditionally and let the caller see a setpoint above the cap. Then extend the smoke grid to include slots in (0, 1, 2, 3) so the choice is pinned.

findings.where: .rework/capture_oracle.py:79-81, 128-133 and the corresponding docstrings in src/spine/derive.py:47-69, 396-435, 348-393
findings.problem:
You asked whether the oracle asserts every case. tests/test_derive.py DOES replay every case in every .json file (575 of them, all passing) -- but the capture GRIDS systematically omit the guard clauses each docstring calls load-bearing, and one docstring cites the table as authority for a case the table does not contain:
  * cull_gate_open: slots values are only (4, 1024, 4096, 8192). The docstring says the slots=0 behaviour is 'preserved because the table says so'. The table has no slots=0 case; the claim has no evidence behind it.
  * blowup_stale: every `recent` in all 36 cases has length 3 and `best` is never None. The `len(recent) < 3` guard -- the one the docstring says is what stops the alarm that fired on 4 healthy runs out of 4 -- and the `best is None` guard are asserted nowhere, table or smoke.
  * curve_verdict: no None inputs in any of the 105 cases, so 2 of the 7 return paths (the whole missing-data branch) never execute in any test.
To separate 'untested' from 'wrong' I differential-fuzzed all eight rebuilt functions against the shipped source lifted by AST from self_organize.py, over a much wider grid including negatives, None, empty sequences and out-of-range widths: 0 disagreements. The reproduction is faithful; only the assertions are a subset.
findings.fix: Extend the grids in .rework/capture_oracle.py to include slots=0 for cull_gate_open, recent lengths 0/1/2 and best=None for blowup_stale, and None for both curve_verdict positions, then re-capture. Where a case cannot be re-captured, move the claim out of the docstring or add it to smoke() as an explicit hand-written assertion labelled as such.

findings.where: src/spine/derive.py:440-489 (phase_schedule), docstring line 446-447
findings.problem:
The docstring states 'Every area enters, is active for a contiguous stretch, and fades.' That is false whenever (n_areas - width) > (n_phases - 1), because the window slides in p-1 steps of size (n_areas-w)/(p-1) and any step larger than 1 jumps over areas:
  phase_schedule(5, 4, 1) -> [[0], [1], [3], [4]]     area 2 is never active in any phase
  phase_schedule(6, 4, 1) -> [[0], [2], [3], [5]]     areas 1 and 4 never active
I checked n in 2..11 across p and width: 130 parameter combinations skip at least one area. (5,4,1) is IN the oracle grid, so this is shipped behaviour faithfully reproduced -- the problem is the comment asserting a property the code does not have, in the function that defines the continual-learning schedule (goal B). A corpus that never trains still shows up in the report's area list, and bwt_of/forgetting_of intersect on shared keys so it enters or leaves the denominator depending on whether it was ever probed. The only test is `phase_schedule(2)[-1] != [0, 1]`, which checks a different property (the last phase excludes someone -- that one I verified holds, 0 violations).
findings.fix: Either correct the docstring to say a wide stride can skip areas and name the condition, or make it a property: raise when n_phases - 1 < n_areas - width, since a schedule that never trains an area cannot support a claim about forgetting it. Add the coverage assertion to smoke(): the union over phases must equal range(n_areas).

findings.where: src/spine/registry.py:27-30 (register) and :216-231 (unread_env)
findings.problem:
_ENV_OWNER is append-only -- register() never retires a name -- so a lever renamed within one process leaves the old environment name permanently 'declared'. Reproduced by defining FAB with `n0` and then redefining it with `nstart` (allowed by the same_class escape at registry.py:195):
  after rename: _ENV_OWNER == {'FAB_N0': 'FAB', 'FAB_NSTART': 'FAB'}
  unread_env({'FAB_N0': '1'}) == []          # the typo net stays silent
FAB_N0 now exists on no class, is read by nothing, is not reported by G9, and affects('FAB_N0') returns {'FAB'} instead of raising -- so the L3 sweep would flip a dead knob, measure no movement, and pass. That is precisely the failure unread_env's docstring names ('a knob corrected in the registry and not at the call site'). Reachable in any process that imports two versions of a set: module reload, the isolation sweep, and test harnesses.
findings.fix: When register() replaces a prior owner for a PREFIX, drop that owner's old env names from _ENV_OWNER before adding the new ones. Separately, have affects() and unread_env() derive their known set from all_sets() live rather than from an accumulated map, so a stale entry cannot survive a re-registration.

findings.where: src/spine/registry.py:224 (unread_env, `fams = tuple(families or ...)`) and src/spine/assemble.py:577-580
findings.problem: unread_env only inspects names that already start with a REGISTERED prefix, so G9 is silent about exactly the two cases most likely to bite. Measured with only FAB registered: FAB_NMAXX is flagged; FBA_NMAX (a typo in the PREFIX itself) is not; TOK_VMAX (a real knob whose package this build did not import) is not; NOPE_X is not. Also, build(sets=<subset>) resolves a subset of packages but the typo net still consults the global registry, so a knob belonging to a package excluded from this build reads as 'declared and fine' when nothing in the run will read it.
findings.fix: Scan with a looser family rule -- any name matching ^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*_ -- and classify: matches a declared lever (fine), close to one (typo, current behaviour), or matches a known-prefix shape with no owner (report as 'no package claims this family; is it imported?'). And in build(), pass the resolved `sets` down so the typo net is computed against the packages this build actually assembled.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:132-138 (Config._wire)
findings.problem: _wire performs a plain dict assignment and permits a silent second write to one field: `c._wire('d_v', 1); c._wire('d_v', 2)` leaves 2, no error. The table path is guarded twice (assemble._check_table and Wires.add both refuse a duplicate destination), but wire.py:251-254 argues that silent overwrite 'is the class that leaves no trace at all in a log' and assemble.py:270-276 argues at length that a guard belongs at the point that performs the assignment. _wire IS that point, and it is the one place with no check.
findings.fix: Raise LeverError in _wire when `name` is already in self._wired (or in self._vals -- see the d_-lever finding), naming the prior value. Three lines, and it makes the two table-level checks defence in depth rather than the only defence.

findings.where: src/spine/lever.py:145-165 (Config.__getattr__ vs the methods and property on Config)
findings.problem: __getattr__ only runs when normal lookup fails, so a lever whose field name matches a Config member is silently unreachable. Reproduced: a set declaring `keys = Lever(5,...)` and `prefix = Lever(7,...)` resolves cfg.keys to the bound method and cfg.prefix to the string 'SH'; the declared values 5 and 7 sit in _vals and cannot be read by attribute access. The same applies to `given`, `wired` and `lever`. Nothing in Lever, LeverSet, registry or test_ownership refuses those names, and the read returns a plausible object rather than failing.
findings.fix: Refuse the reserved names at declaration time in __init_subclass__ (a small frozenset checked against the field names), with an error that lists them. Cheaper and more honest than renaming the introspection API.

findings.where: src/spine/rng.py:252-260 (spawn), 265-286 (torch_generator), 288-297 (numpy_generator), 192 (_ISSUED write), 326 (issued)
findings.problem: Two related gaps in the G4 three-state ledger. (1) torch_generator() and numpy_generator() derive seeds under '<name>.torch' / '<name>.numpy' but never register in _ISSUED, so issued() -- documented as 'Every stream handed out in this process' and used by the report to distinguish 'armed but inert' from 'never asked' -- reports a subsystem whose only randomness is a torch generator as never having asked. tests/test_determinism.py's reference workload does exactly this (fab.torch_generator()). (2) spawn('torch') derives the identical seed to torch_generator(): both are derive_seed(name + '.torch', run_seed) -- verified equal -- which is the same-integer-beside-two-streams confusion torch_generator's own docstring says the sub-name avoids.
findings.fix: Register the derived interop seeds in _ISSUED under their full sub-name (they are streams handed out), and reserve 'torch'/'numpy' as child names in _check_name when called from spawn(), so the two paths cannot collide.

findings.where: src/spine/rng.py:212-244 (shuffle, sample, choices, gauss) against the class docstring at :168-170
findings.problem: The Rng docstring says '.draws is counted for the report's three-state DID IT FIRE line ... a fact about the run rather than an estimate', and the per-method comment repeats 'what it buys is that .draws is a fact about the run rather than an estimate'. It is a CALL count, not a draw count: shuffle(list of 50) records 49 while random.shuffle makes 49 variable-cost _randbelow calls; sample(pop, k) records k; gauss() records 1 while consuming one or two underlying draws (the fingerprint() comment already acknowledges the gauss case). Only zero-vs-nonzero is used today so no number moves, but the comment is load-bearing under this codebase's own rules and it overstates what the counter is.
findings.fix: Say what it is -- 'calls made through this stream, not underlying generator draws; the report uses only zero vs non-zero' -- or count real draws by diffing the generator position, which is available via getstate() at no draw cost.

findings.where: census `## domains` section vs self_organize.py:96-513 (_SPEC) — DOM_FOLD_MULT :243/:648/:3624, DOM_RECUR_HORIZON :276/:647/:3614, DOM_PRIOR :249/:658/:6788/:7785/:8147, TOKC_DECAY :250/:664/:7786, SEG_MIN :291/:1406, SEG_MAX :290/:1410
findings.problem: Six of the 37 knobs tagged `# domains` in _SPEC are absent from the census entirely — no keep/rename/merge/drop verdict, no line, nothing. I extracted _SPEC programmatically: fabric 91/91 covered (92 rows, the extra being FAB_MIN_STEPS, correctly flagged), misc 41/41 covered, domains only 31/37. Missing: DOM_FOLD_MULT, DOM_RECUR_HORIZON, DOM_PRIOR, TOKC_DECAY, SEG_MIN, SEG_MAX. All six are live (every one has at least one non-declaration read site) and all six carry survey lever records in .rework/survey/so-config.json, so none can be excused as undiscovered. This is exactly the outcome G10 exists to prevent: 'a lever disappearing without a decision'. It also breaks P2's stated verification, 'every old knob appears exactly once in the census; count reconciles' — the count does not reconcile, it is short by six.
findings.fix: Add a census row for each of the six. Note two of them are already known-misfiled and the survey says so verbatim: SEG_MIN and SEG_MAX are recorded as 'registry says domains; is a data/stream knob' — they parameterise `random.randint(SEG_MIN, SEG_MAX)` inside build_stream at :1406/:1410, so they belong to DATA, not DOM, and they carry restated call-site defaults at :1406, :1410 and :5707 (an L1 violation to record at port). DOM_PRIOR is not obviously DOM-owned either: it blends a per-domain token histogram into the LM prediction at :8187, so its owner is arguably EVAL or LM with the histogram arriving as a wire.

findings.where: census row `DOM_RECUR [1] -> rename DOM.fold (on/off)` vs self_organize.py:3613-3624
findings.problem: The census keeps the recurrence fold — calling it 'the first thing in the project's history that passed that test' — while both of the fold's parameters are among the six missing knobs, so the mechanism ships with no guard and no clock. Read the loop: `drop = [i for i in s.cent if s.visits.get(i,0) < DOM_MIN_VISITS and s.nb - s.bornb.get(i, s.nb) >= DOM_RECUR_HORIZON]` (:3613-3614), then `if not s._radp or 1 - float(sm[k]) > DOM_FOLD_MULT * s._radp: ds.discard(b); continue` (:3624). The census censuses DOM_MIN_VISITS and omits the other two. DOM_FOLD_MULT is the fold's only safety guard and its declaration comment at :648 states the failure without it in as many words — 'refuse to fold further than this x the pooled radius (unguarded -> 1 domain)' — and the inline comment at :3621-3623 repeats it: 'an unbounded fold collapses the whole population to one domain'. The census's own DOM_RECUR row even names DOM_FOLD_MULT ('Renamed to `fold` so DOM_FOLD/DOM_FOLD_MULT read as one mechanism') and then never gives it a row, and the survey's DOM_RECUR record lists couples_with = ['DOM_MIN_VISITS','DOM_RECUR_HORIZON','DOM_FOLD_MULT'] — two of three silently gone.
findings.fix: Census DOM_FOLD_MULT as DOM.fold_mult (kept; it is the guard, not decoration) and DOM_RECUR_HORIZON as DOM.fold_horizon. Note DOM_RECUR_HORIZON's clock has no kind in the frozen units.py: it counts BOUNDARIES (`s.nb - s.bornb[i]`), and Steps/Flushes/Windows/Backwards/Epochs/Selections do not include boundaries. Either it gets a Boundaries clock or it must be documented as an untyped count with the reason, the same treatment DECAY_EVERY correctly got.

findings.where: census rows `CHAIN_DEPTH0 -> rename FAB.FAB_DEPTH0` and `FAB_MIN_STEPS -> merge FAB.FAB_DEPTH0` vs self_organize.py:2609 and :2713
findings.problem: The merge collapses a ceiling and a floor into one field, on a stated equivalence that the source contradicts. FAB_MIN_STEPS is a LOWER bound: `if _t_ < s.min_steps:` blocks HALT for the first k hops (:2713). CHAIN_DEPTH0 is an UPPER bound: `steps = max(1, min(s.depth_now, s.max_steps, 2 + N // 2))` where `s.depth_now = int(_env('CHAIN_DEPTH0',1)) if s.curric else max_steps` (:1802, :2609), and it GROWS toward max_steps as the curriculum advances (:2535). The census asserts FAB_MIN_STEPS 'expresses the same intent (at least this many hops)' — it does not; FAB_DEPTH0 means 'at MOST this many hops, to begin with'. After the merge there is no way to express 'start the staged curriculum at depth 1' and 'always take at least 2 hops before HALT is allowed' as the two independent facts they are, and the census's own FAB_HALT row depends on HALT-blocking being a live control.
findings.fix: Keep FAB_MIN_STEPS as its own lever (FAB.min_hops, a floor) and FAB_DEPTH0 as the curriculum start ceiling. The census's real finding about FAB_MIN_STEPS is sound and should be kept as its help text: its declared derived default never executes because :1868 sets `s.min_steps = 0` unconditionally under CHAIN_VOTE=1 and SystemExits only on an explicit conflicting env value (:1861-1867), which is the banner lie recorded at :30-32. That argues for a declared derivation from FAB_HOP_VOTE, not for a merge into a different quantity.

findings.where: census rows `FAB_NORM_ONLY [0] -> merge FAB.FAB_MODE (on/off)` and `FABRIC [1] -> rename FAB.FAB_ON (on/off)`
findings.problem: FAB_NORM_ONLY is merged into a target, FAB.FAB_MODE, that has no census row and that the census elsewhere contradicts. Its body says 'Merged into the fabric master switch (FABRIC, currently tagged misc, owner FAB) as a third choice -- on / off / norm-only' — i.e. FABRIC becomes a three-armed name lever. But the FABRIC row censuses it as `rename FAB.FAB_ON (on/off)` and says it 'Keeps its meaning', a two-state flag. One of the two rows must be wrong, and as written the merge lands nowhere. The unit tag on the FAB_NORM_ONLY row is also '(on/off)' while the body describes three arms, which under the frozen lever.py matters concretely: `Lever.coerce` branches on the Python type of the default, so a bool/int default cannot carry `choices={'on','off','norm_only'}` and the enumerated-arm behaviour the row asks for would not exist.
findings.fix: Pick one. Either FABRIC's row becomes `rename FAB.FAB_MODE (name, choices={on,off,norm_only})` with FAB_NORM_ONLY merging into it, or FAB_NORM_ONLY stays a separate flag. The census's substantive point — that there are two different ways to say 'no fabric' and they differ in ways nothing states (FABRIC=0 removes it from the forward pass; norm_only leaves the object built, its parameters in the optimizer and its state in the checkpoint, re-tested at six call sites as `not fab.norm_only`) — is correct and argues for the three-way, so FABRIC's row is the one to change.

findings.where: whole census, `## fabric` and `## misc` sections (~130 rows), vs src/spine/lever.py Lever.env_name and src/spine/assemble.py:285,339,393
findings.problem: The fabric and misc sections name target fields as `FAB.FAB_N0`, `FAB.FAB_AE_W`, `MEM.MEM_TOPK`, `EVAL.EVAL_AFF_MIN`, `TOK.TOK_GROW_EVERY`, `DATA.DATA_VAL_CAP`, `SIG.SIG_TEMP` — i.e. PREFIX.PREFIX_FIELD. Taken literally as field names on a LeverSet, lever.py generates `f"{self.prefix}_{self.name.upper()}"`, so these produce doubled env names. I ran it: a LeverSet with PREFIX='FAB' and a field `FAB_N0` yields env_names {'FAB_FAB_N0','FAB_FAB_NMAX','FAB_FAB_DEPTH_PATIENCE'}; PREFIX='MEM' with field `MEM_TOPK` yields 'MEM_MEM_TOPK'. The `## domains` section uses the correct form (DOM.enabled, DOM.spawn_dist, DOM.accept_rule → DOM_ENABLED, DOM_SPAWN_DIST, DOM_ACCEPT_RULE), so the census is internally inconsistent about the one rule it most often cites as its justification for a rename ('the env name must be PREFIX_FIELD', CHAIN_PATIENCE row). Worse, src/spine/assemble.py already fixes the field names for three of these: FAB_NMAX is `FAB.slots` (:285, :302, :324, :393), FAB_PRESSURE is `FAB.pressure` (:393), MANAGE_EVERY is `FAB.manage_every` (:339). So the census's fabric rows contradict already-written, already-passing spine code.
findings.fix: Rewrite the fabric and misc rows in the domains section's form: field name without the prefix, env name shown separately. State the resolved env name in the row so it is checkable. Reconcile with assemble.py's existing field names (slots, pressure, manage_every) or change assemble.py deliberately — but the census must say which, because O4 in tests/test_ownership.py binds the wire destinations to those names.

findings.where: census rows `MAX_DOMAINS -> promote-to-wire FAB.d_expert_slots` and `EVAL_GIST -> promote-to-wire SIG.d_eval_gist`, vs src/spine/assemble.py:283-284 and :424-433 (NOT_WIRES)
findings.problem: Both promote-to-wire rows put the `d_` field on the SOURCE package instead of the receiver, inverting the direction their own bodies state. For MAX_DOMAINS the header says `FAB.d_expert_slots` while the body says 'As a wire it lands on DOM as d_expert_slots' — and assemble.py already declares it correctly as src='FAB.slots', dst='DOM.d_expert_slots'. A `d_` field on FAB would mean FAB receives its own slot count from elsewhere. Under lever.py's `Config._wire` and test_ownership O4, `dst` is the receiver, so the census as written declares a wire that cannot exist. For EVAL_GIST the header says `SIG.d_eval_gist` while the body says 'eval receives it as a d_-prefixed wire' — destination should be EVAL. This is a second, worse problem: assemble.py's NOT_WIRES already REJECTS a SIG-side signature wire by name, with the reason ('SIG.d_signature_width_bytes from DATA.win x the measured bytes/token' — 'Not resolvable at assemble: bytes_per_token is MEASURED on the corpus the tokenizer has not seen yet... derive.signature_width_bytes is the single named function instead'). The census proposes the thing the spine has already written down a rejection for, without citing or answering that rejection.
findings.fix: Flip both destinations: `DOM.d_expert_slots` (already declared — the census row should say 'already wired at assemble.py:283' rather than proposing it) and `EVAL.d_eval_gist` / `EVAL.d_signature_width_bytes`. For EVAL_GIST, reconcile against assemble.py's NOT_WIRES entry: if the width is resolved by derive.signature_width_bytes and carried on the Sample, then EVAL_GIST is a plain drop, not a wire, and the row should say so.

findings.where: census row `MANAGE_EVERY [500] -> rename FAB.manage_every (Windows)` vs src/spine/assemble.py:339
findings.problem: The census types MANAGE_EVERY as Windows; assemble.py already types it as Steps — `derive.flush_period(Steps(r['FAB'].manage_every), r['TRAIN'].batch_w)` — with a `why` that asserts 'MANAGE_EVERY is written in STEPS'. They cannot both be right and the census does not flag the conflict. The source says the census is correct: `step` advances only alongside `i += WIN` at :6796 and :7708, so `step % MANAGE_EVERY == 0` at :6716, :6764, :6768 and :6769 is a WINDOW comparison. Under the frozen units.py, Steps is documented as 'Optimizer steps... and nothing else', so assemble.py is carrying a live unit mismatch of exactly the class it was written to kill. I confirmed the static check cannot see this: tests/test_ownership.py O7 passes (107 comparisons examined, 0 failing) because `Steps(<int>)` is a legal construction — the wrong kind is chosen at the constructor, which is upstream of every comparison O7 inspects.
findings.fix: Have the census state the conflict explicitly and resolve it: change assemble.py's coupling to `Windows(r['FAB'].manage_every).convert(Flushes, per=batch_w)` (the arithmetic is already right — windows-per-flush IS batch_w, matching the shipped `MANAGE_EVERY // BATCH_W` at :6819/:6836/:6961/:6988/:7077/:7325 — only the kind is wrong), and rewrite the `why` string, which currently teaches the wrong unit. Also record that O7 is blind to a mis-kinded constructor, since the census leans on the Clock types as the remedy for this whole family.

findings.where: census row `ROUTE_GROUNDED [1] -> drop FAB. (on/off)` vs self_organize.py:2603, :2634, :2400-2426
findings.problem: The drop rests on 'No region term is already expressible by FAB_ROUTE_REGION_W=0', and that equivalence is false. `ground_update` is called only under `if s.grounded and ban1 is None and learn_regions:` (:2603 and :2634). Setting FAB_ROUTE_REGION_W=0 zeroes the region term inside entry_logits but leaves ground_update running at full cost — and that is the loop the census itself flags under FAB_CENT_TOPK as ISSUES M35: each of the k centroids is written back with `.cpu()` and `float(_share[_q5])` forces a host sync, 'dozens of device/host synchronisations per training step' (:2411-2426). FAB_DISCOVER's only call site is inside that same block (:2421-2424), so ROUTE_GROUNDED=0 is also the only switch that turns discovery off. The drop therefore removes the sole off-switch for a measured performance defect and for a second mechanism, and the census records neither loss.
findings.fix: Either keep an arm that skips ground_update (e.g. fold it into FAB_CENT_TOPK=0 or a declared Gate), or amend the row to state plainly that FAB_ROUTE_REGION_W=0 is NOT equivalent and that the M35 sync cost becomes unconditional. Separately, the row should record what keeping grounded-only makes load-bearing: `cent` is a registered buffer precisely because as a plain attribute it 'was absent from state_dict(), so the GROUNDED router's centroids -- which ARE the routing function when ROUTE_GROUNDED=1 -- were never saved, never resumed' (:1662-1665). With the alternative router gone, that buffer is the whole routing function across every resume.

findings.where: census row `FAB_NMAX [4096] -> keep FAB.FAB_NMAX` vs src/spine/assemble.py:281-333 and .rework/survey/*.json FAB_NMAX records
findings.problem: The couples_with is badly incomplete for the single most-wired lever in the tree. The row names only FAB_PRESSURE and an instrument defect (M115). It omits: the three memory couplings assemble.py ALREADY declares from this exact lever — MEM.d_owner_blocks (:300), MEM.d_capacity (:311), MEM.d_source_slots (:322), two of them marked irreducible, one of them carrying the measured 24x capacity shrink; GROW_CAP_FAB0, which appears in six of the seven survey records for FAB_NMAX and whose _SPEC comment is '0 = start at FAB_NMAX', i.e. a computed default reading this knob; and RESUME, since FAB_NMAX is in the checkpoint geometry gate at :4442-4468. The census gives FAB_DK the checkpoint-compatibility treatment ('resuming with a different FAB_DK invalidates every identity... in the rebuild that refusal is CKPT's, reading FAB_DK as a wire') and then does not give the same treatment to FAB_NMAX, which sits in the same gate and additionally sizes A and B.
findings.fix: Rewrite the row's coupling list to name the four already-declared or already-known edges (DOM.d_expert_slots, MEM.d_owner_blocks, MEM.d_capacity, MEM.d_source_slots), add GROW_CAP_FAB0 as a computed-default to be resolved when the capacity family is censused, and add FAB_NMAX to the checkpoint-compatibility set alongside FAB_DK and FAB_EMB_HID.

findings.where: census rows `FAB_RAMP_RATE [0.10] -> drop` and `FAB_RAMP_TO [0.5] -> drop`, vs self_organize.py:2909-2919
findings.problem: Two problems. (a) FAB_RAMP_RATE's drop is supported by the forbidden argument: 'It has never taken effect at the shipped defaults, because FAB_RAMP_TO=0.5 ... latches the ramp on its first call -- ramp firings measured at 0'. That is a knob that never fired because another lever's setting made it unreachable — the identical shape the census correctly refuses to accept for FAB_BALANCE ('the quantity it multiplies is a freshly allocated zero scalar'), FAB_RESCUE, FAB_LR_CYCLE, CHAIN_DEPTH0 and CHAIN_SUP. (b) FAB_RAMP_TO's drop claims the ramp makes 'the continual-learning growth path unreachable by construction', but the cited measurement at :2910-2912 shows REGRESSION = 0 in ALL THREE arms, including ramp_to=0.5 with the ramp fully off: 'ramp 0, REGRESSION 0, stall 7'. Removing the ramp demonstrably does not restore the regression trigger. The source names the actual cause two lines later (:2917-2921): REGRESSION and stall share one cooldown through `s.last`, and the injected regression was dropped on `t - s.last = 772 < cool = 1500`. The census records that under FAB_COOLDOWN but does not connect it, so the ramp removal is sold on an outcome the data does not show.
findings.fix: Strike the never-fired clause from FAB_RAMP_RATE and let it ride purely on FAB_RAMP_TO's mechanism removal, which is honest evidence (417 firings, and the firing was the damage). Amend FAB_RAMP_TO to state that after the ramp is dropped REGRESSION still measured 0, and that the fix that actually unblocks on-demand growth is splitting `s.last` per trigger — otherwise the rebuild ships with no working continual-learning growth path and a census row claiming it was restored.

findings.where: census row `FAB_N0 [2048] -> keep FAB.FAB_N0` vs self_organize.py:2923-2925
findings.problem: The row quotes 'the 2x2 at cc0a377' and gives three of its four arms: GROW=0 N0=3 → 2.117/0.326, GROW=0 N0=2048 → 1.999/0.080, GROW=1 NMAX=4096 → 3.384/2.074. The source table has a fourth arm the census omits: `GROW=1 NMAX=64   2.091, spread 0.180` (:2925). That arm is the one that bears on the configuration the census actually ships. With it, the table says growth is fine at a small cap and the damage is specific to growth against a large cap; without it, the table reads as 'growth is bad'. The census keeps FAB_GROW=1 and FAB_NMAX=4096 — precisely the 3.384 / spread 2.074 arm — and does not say so. Calling a three-arm excerpt 'the 2x2' also misdescribes the design.
findings.fix: Quote all four arms, and add the consequence to the FAB_NMAX and FAB_GROW rows: the only clean growth-on arm in the record ran at NMAX=64, so shipping GROW=1 with NMAX=4096 is the untested-at-this-scale combination and needs to be a named arm in the isolation sweep rather than an unremarked default. Keep the census's own caveat that these are pre-fix signals, not facts.

findings.where: census rows `EXPERT_NULLS [20] -> merge EVAL.EVAL_NULL_DRAWS` and `INFO_NULLS [5] -> rename EVAL.EVAL_NULL_DRAWS`
findings.problem: Two levers with different defaults are merged into one field and neither row states which default survives. Every other merge in the census resolves this explicitly — EXPERT_CULL_RANK ('The 0.08 value is not carried over'), EXPERT_GRACE ('The 3000 does not carry over'), EXPERT_NEW_DIST ('Merge into FAB_DISCOVER (0.35)'), EXPERT_PRESSURE (into 0.45) — so the omission is out of character and leaves the merged lever with no literal default, which lever.py forbids outright at declaration time. The 4x gap is also not arbitrary: the two nulls have very different per-draw costs (a permutation of expert assignments at :9171 versus a compose_test rebuild at :3831), so one number now has to serve two cost/resolution tradeoffs.
findings.fix: State the surviving default and the reason. If the two costs genuinely differ by enough that one number cannot serve both, this is a rename-both-separately, not a merge — and the census should say that instead. Either way keep the floor the rows correctly ask for, which makes ISSUES L44 (INFO_NULLS=0 → ZeroDivisionError) and L45 (=1 → the 2-sigma test is a rubber stamp) unrepresentable.

findings.where: census row `FAB_BALANCE [0.01] -> keep FAB.FAB_BALANCE` vs .rework/ISSUES.md:29-32 (C2) and _SPEC:BAL_WARM/BAL_FLOOR (tagged optim)
findings.problem: The row keeps FAB_BALANCE, correctly, as the broken-wiring case — but it never mentions BAL_WARM (4000) and BAL_FLOOR (0.15), the two knobs that parameterise the same mechanism and that _SPEC files under `optim`, a different family. ISSUES C2, which the census cites for this very row, names all three together: 'FAB_BALANCE, BAL_WARM and BAL_FLOOR are read, printed in the config banner and reasoned about at length'. The survey's FAB_GRACE record also lists BAL_FLOOR in couples_with. Under L2 a FAB function cannot read an OPT lever, so keeping FAB_BALANCE under FAB without declaring how BAL_WARM and BAL_FLOOR arrive leaves the mechanism with two-thirds of its parameters in a package that cannot legally reach it.
findings.fix: Add the coupling to the row now, even though the optim family is outside this census slice — either as a note that BAL_WARM/BAL_FLOOR must move to FAB when optim is censused, or as declared wires. A cross-slice dependency that neither slice records is how the original _SPEC drifted.

findings.where: census rows `COMP_EMA -> rename FAB.FAB_COMP_EMA` and `COMP_PROTECT -> rename FAB.FAB_COMP_PROTECT` vs self_organize.py:6932, :6720, :2235-2239, :3694
findings.problem: The census resolves the L2 conflict for the RATE (FAB owns it, domains get d_comp_ema) but never declares the wire for the VALUE that makes the rate meaningful. `asm.comp_glob` is computed on the domain assembler at :6932 and then passed INTO the fabric — `fab.manage(..., comp_glob=asm.comp_glob, ...)` at :6720 — where it is the comparison baseline for the spare rule at :2235-2239, and it is separately the baseline for the domain cull at :3694. So the direction is DOM → FAB for the baseline while the census wires FAB → DOM for the rate. One of the two crossings is declared and the other is not, which under G5 means `grep d_` will not enumerate it.
findings.fix: Declare the second edge explicitly (DOM.comp_glob → FAB.d_population_competence, or move the whole competence bookkeeping to one owner). The census's COMP_PROTECT row already identifies this field as the ARMED predicate for the fabric.spare and fabric.failed_out audit rows at :8569-8573, which under G4 must become a Gate reading named inputs — and a Gate cannot read an undeclared cross-package value.

findings.where: census row `EVICT [lru] -> rename MEM.MEM_EVICT (name)` vs memory.py:25, :242, :287
findings.problem: The row says 'Keep all three arms; declare them as choices' without naming the third, and misses a second literal default. (a) memory.py:25's constructor signature is `evict="recency"` while self_organize.py:4871 passes `_env("EVICT","lru")` — two different defaults for one knob, the exact L1 violation the census catches elsewhere (FAB_NEW_WIN, MAX_DOMAINS). The row does not record it. (b) The arms are not where the row implies. memory.py:287 splits only `usage` from everything-else (`self.use[cand] if self.evict == "usage" else self.last[cand].float()`), but the real gate is :242, `if self.evict in ("usage","lru") and int(self.active.sum()) >= self.cap:` — so the third arm is the unnamed else branch that bypasses ranked eviction entirely. A `choices=` set cannot be written until that third value has a name.
findings.fix: Name the three arms explicitly and pick the surviving default, recording that memory.py:25's 'recency' must be deleted rather than carried. The row's substantive point about ISSUES M24 (unrecognised string values falling into the else branch, shared with SIG_MODE, CULL_MODE, CHAIN_ROUTE and eight others) is right and is the reason the enumeration has to be complete rather than gestural.

findings.where: census row `MERGE_FRAC [0.8] -> merge DOM.merge_dist` vs self_organize.py:3643 and src/spine/lever.py Lever.__init__
findings.problem: The row simultaneously removes MERGE_FRAC and retains it: 'The design intent survives as an intra-package derived default (d_merge_dist = frac * spawn_dist resolved once in spine.derive and printed), not as a second settable knob'. But `frac` in that expression has to come from somewhere. If it is still a lever, MERGE_FRAC was not merged; if it is a literal, the row should say which literal and that 0.8 is now frozen. As written the rebuild would have both a declared `merge_dist` lever (0.28) and a derived `d_merge_dist`, with nothing saying which one the merge loop reads — reproducing at the spine level the same two-routes-to-one-number defect the row is removing. Note also that lever.py refuses a non-literal default outright ('A value derived from another lever is a WIRE, not a default'), so 'derived default' is not an available category.
findings.fix: State it one way: either merge_dist is the only lever and 0.8 disappears entirely (the row's evidence supports this — `md = merge_dist if merge_dist > 0 else MERGE_FRAC * NEW_DIST` at :3643 means the product is unreachable at any non-zero merge_dist, and 0.28 happens to equal 0.8 x 0.35 by coincidence), or d_merge_dist replaces the lever and merge_dist stops being settable. Not both.

findings.where: census row `FAB_PRESS_SOFT [0] -> drop FAB. (on/off)`
findings.problem: The drop is argued as 'a gate must have one denominator, chosen once', and then the row chooses the denominator it was removing the ability to choose: 'The rebuild measures pressure against the operating cap growth is actually clamped by'. That operating cap is the capacity valve's soft cap — GROW_CAP_FAB / GROW_CAP_FAB0, tagged `capacity` in _SPEC and not present in this census slice. So dropping FAB_PRESS_SOFT does not remove the coupling to the capacity package, it hard-wires it, and it does so from a slice that cannot see the owning family's rows. This also silently settles the FAB_PRESSURE/FAB_NMAX setpoint that PLAN section 4 and assemble.py:391-403 build the irreducible-coupling example on, since d_operating_population is currently `pressure x slots` and would now have to be `pressure x soft_cap`.
findings.fix: Hold the FAB_PRESS_SOFT verdict until the capacity family is censused, or state the consequence explicitly and amend assemble.py's FAB.d_operating_population coupling in the same breath. The row's diagnosis (ISSUES M39: the printed arithmetic uses fab.cap while fab.manage was given `_cap_fab[0]`) is correct and is a reason to print the gate's real denominator under G4, which does not by itself require dropping the arm.

findings.where: census row `DIV_MASS [1] -> drop FAB. (on/off)` read against its own `DIV_W` row
findings.problem: DIV_MASS is dropped on a purely theoretical argument ('the reward is largest exactly where it is meaningless') with no measurement of either arm, while the adjacent DIV_W row records that the society-path DIV_W site 'indexed a rank slot with a global expert id and raised IndexError the first time anyone set it above zero (:7038-7042) -- a crash nobody met because of a default'. If DIV_W above zero has never run on that path, then the weighted and unweighted forms of the differentiation reward have never been compared, on either path. The census's own standard elsewhere (FAB_EC_W: 'Dropping the alternative while the incumbent is unmeasured would leave the balance question with no arm to test against') applies exactly here and reaches the opposite conclusion.
findings.fix: Either keep DIV_MASS as an arm until DIV_W has run once on a path where it does not crash, or state in the row that the two arms were never compared and that the drop is a design ruling rather than an evidenced one — the census is careful to make that distinction elsewhere and should here.

findings.where: census row `DOM_CULL_EMPTY [1] -> drop DOM. (on/off)` vs self_organize.py:3626-3641, :8637-8639
findings.problem: The row asserts 'it fires, and its off state is a known-untrippable guard', but cites no firing count, and the only number it does cite argues the other way: 'the pilot log shows zero culls for 1000 steps against 5-8 merges per pass'. In the source that observation (:3629-3630) is the SYMPTOM the empty-cull was added to fix, describing the old act/stale conjunction, not evidence about DOM_CULL_EMPTY itself. A dedicated counter exists (`s.emptied`, :3641) and is surfaced as the `domains.empty` DID IT FIRE row at :8637-8639, so a real number is available and none is given. Dropping the off-arm of a mechanism on an assertion is thin, given the owner's ruling that firing evidence is what settles these.
findings.fix: Quote the `s.emptied` / domains.empty count from a run, or soften the row to 'behaviour made unconditional because the gated operation is lossless by construction (no windows AND no memory entries AND past grace)', which is the argument that actually carries and does not depend on a firing count. The row's separate point — that dropping it removes one of the three DID IT FIRE armed-predicates pointing at a crashing `step % 0` value (:8638) — is correct and independent.

findings.where: census row `EXPERT_MERGE_DIST [0.10] -> rename FAB.FAB_MERGE_DIST`
findings.problem: This is a conditional verdict, not a classification: 'Carried over as FAB_MERGE_DIST on the explicit condition that the fabric gains the merge; if that mechanism is not ported at P3 this must return to the census as a drop rather than ship as an inert default.' G10 requires all 328 knobs classified kept/renamed/merged/dropped and P2's verification is that the count reconciles; a verdict contingent on a future implementation choice reconciles to neither column. If the condition fails the census ships a lever with no reader — the recorded-never-read class it drops WRONG_MARGIN, WRONG_MIN_N and WRONG_THRESH for.
findings.fix: Resolve it now. The reasoning for keeping it is strong and goal-B-relevant (ExpertRouter.manage at :3063-3085 averages two adapters and sums their use, so 'both experts' learning survives'; Fabric.manage does cull and spare only; the domain population already merges via MANAGE_MERGE, so the fabric is the odd one out) — so make porting the fabric merge a P3 deliverable and classify this as kept, or classify it as dropped with the mechanism recorded in docs/dropped_levers.md as a proposed addition. A tracked open item is fine; an unresolved census row is not.

findings.where: census unit column across merge rows; and _SPEC type tags at self_organize.py:472-473 and the 44 knobs typed 'env' with numeric defaults
findings.problem: Two typing gaps that matter under the frozen lever.py, where `Lever.coerce` branches on the Python type of the default and the `unit` argument is pure metadata that changes nothing. (a) Merge rows show the SOURCE knob's unit rather than the target's: `CHAIN_CURRIC -> merge FAB.FAB_DEPTH0 (on/off)` where FAB_DEPTH0 is a count, `WRITE_QUANTILE -> merge MEM.MEM_WRITE_MODE (on/off)` where the target is a name, `FAB_NORM_ONLY -> merge FAB.FAB_MODE (on/off)` where the body describes three arms. Since the census's unit column is what feeds docs/04_LEVERS.md, these will land wrong. (b) The census assigns unit `on/off` to many knobs without stating the Python type, and the type is what decides behaviour: `Lever(1, ..., U.FLAG).coerce('off')` raises LeverError via `int(float('off'))`, while `Lever(True, ...).coerce('off')` returns False. BIRTH_JITTER and CENT_EMA are additionally typed `('env', 0.15)` and `('env', 0.02)` in _SPEC — string type, numeric default — and are read as `float(_env(...))` at :1921 and :1924; the census's rows type them FRACTION but never record the correction.
findings.fix: Put the TARGET's unit on merge rows, and add a Python-type column (or state the literal default in the row, which implies the type). Record the BIRTH_JITTER/CENT_EMA _SPEC mis-typing in their rows — it is the same class of drift the census exists to catch, and there are 44 knobs typed 'env' with non-string defaults to sweep for at port.
